compute.reported_as: Figure 2 depicts a typical GO process for the Heisenberg model on a 10 x 10 square lattice with D=8. We start from an approximate ground state obtained by SU. In the first 50 GO steps, we set delta_t(n) = 0.005, and gradually increase MC sampling number from M=50000 to M=100000. We reduce delta_t slowly from 0.005 to 0.001 in the next 50 GO steps using delta_t(n+1) = delta_t(n) * 0.968, and gradually increase M. In the last 20 steps, we use fixed delta_t=0.001, and the maximum M=500000. It takes about 25 minutes for each GO step using 500 Intel E5-2860 cores for the maximum M. || TABLE II: Comparison of the ground state energies of the Heisenberg model calculated by PEPS with available exact results for L = 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. The PEPS are optimized via the GO method, with D=8, and Dc=16. (...) [rows D=8 and D=10; L=10: D=10 -0.628601(2); L=16: D=10 -0.643391(3)] || In all these calculations, we use Dc=2D, which converges the results very well, as discussed in Appendix A. || TABLE III: (...) MC+GO: scaling O(M D^6), max D 10, max L 16, relative error ~ 10^-4. || The numerical calculations have been done on the USTC HPC facilities. || Sec. II: "where A^{s_{i,j}}_{i,j} = A_{i,j}(l, r, u, d, s_{i,j}) is a five-index tensor located on site (i,j). It has one physical index s_{i,j} whose value is from 1 to d and four virtual indices l, r, u, d corresponding to four nearest neighbors. The dimension of each virtual bond is D, except for those on open edges, whose dimensions are set to one. [...] The number of the parameters in the PEPS is determined by the bond dimension D." || Eq. (6): "A^{s_m}_{lrud}(n+1) = A^{s_m}_{lrud}(n) - p * delta_t(n) * sign(dE/dA^{s_m}_{lrud}), where p is a random real number ranged from 0 to 1 for each A^{s_m}_{lrud}" || Table II: D = 10 energies for L = 10 (-0.628601(2)) and L = 16 (-0.643391(3))

compute.note: Row is the D = 10 gradient-optimized PEPS energy for L = 16 (open boundaries) from Table II. The only timing statement in the paper ("about 25 minutes for each GO step using 500 Intel E5-2860 cores for the maximum M") is for the 10x10, D = 8 example of Fig. 2, i.e. a different bond dimension and size; it is recorded here at ansatz scope with low confidence. samples = maximum Monte Carlo sampling number M = 500000 (final 20 steps; M grows from 50000 during the run); iterations = 50 + 50 + 20 GO steps of that example (sum of stated stages). "Intel E5-2860" is quoted as printed. Cut-off bond dimension Dc = 2D = 20 for D = 10 (Table II caption says Dc = 16 for D = 8). Total wall-clock and core-hours not stated. || route2a 2026-09-24: parameters = 4032800 evaluated from the stated finite-PEPS definition: one independent tensor per site (the GO update Eq. (6) acts on each site's A^{s_m}_{lrud} separately), d = 2, D = 10, open-edge bonds of dimension 1: 4 corners x d D^2 + 4(L-2) edges x d D^3 + (L-2)^2 bulk x d D^4 = 4 x 200 + 56 x 2000 + 196 x 20000 for L = 16. Real tensor elements (the update uses the sign of the derivative and a random real p). Size-dependent (grows ~ 2 D^4 N). No count is printed in the paper to cross-check. Existing samples/iterations (M = 500000 maximum, 120 GO steps) are the stated protocol of the 10x10 D = 8 example (Fig. 2), not this D = 10 L = 16 run - kept at ansatz scope, low confidence, as before. This row cannot take the nqs-v1 FLOP model: a PEPS amplitude is a boundary-MPS contraction, cost O(D^4 Dc^2) per sample with Dc = 2D (stated), not 2 x parameters. Parameter count on its own: confidence medium (evaluated from the stated definition); block confidence stays low because samples/iterations are from the D = 8 example.

compute.reported_as: Appendix B.3 Optimization: In our experiments we employ the following general optimization strategy. We begin using the Adam [24] SGD variant, using a small batch of 100 samples for estimating the gradient and using a learning rate in the order of 10^−3. After about 10K gradient update steps, we increase the batch size to 1000, using the same learning rate and optimizer as the first stage, for an additional 10K update steps. In the final stage of the optimization, we increase the batch size again, and also switch to standard SGD with a momentum term, for an additional 5K update steps. For each experiment, we test multiple variations around the above default values of batch size, learning rate, and number of update steps in each stage, and report the results for the best performing models. ... Appendix B.1: The 'vertical' containing convolutional layers with 3 × 3 filters and 32 channels ... For the 'horizontal' branch, we use convolutional layers with 3 × 3 filters and 32 channels ... We typically use between 10 and 40 such blocks, depending on the specific experiment. ... Discussion: our direct sampling approach allows us to train very large convolutional networks (20 layers, 21×21 lattice, ∼1M parameters). ... Fig. 3 caption (MCMC comparison): Since MCMC takes a considerable time to complete just a single iteration, we have restricted the training to maximum of 100 hours.

compute.note: Only a generic three-stage optimization recipe is given (Adam, batch 100 for ~10K steps, then batch 1000 for 10K steps, then a larger unspecified batch with SGD+momentum for 5K steps; ~25K updates total) with the caveat that the reported model is the best of several variations, so iterations and samples are left null. Architecture: PixelCNN-style blocks with 3×3 convolutions and 32 channels, 10-40 blocks (the depth used for the 16×16 Heisenberg run is not stated); the '~1M parameters, 20 layers' figure refers to the largest 21×21 experiment, not this row. No hardware, GPU count or wall-clock stated for the NAQS runs; the '100 hours' cap applies to the MCMC baseline training in Fig. 3.
